_note: Hand-authored research trajectories. Each session's final question is held out and must be recovered by the predictor. 'summaries' are what the first three answers taught, mirroring what the real store would hold.
_split: Prompt and format changes are tuned on dev. Test is scored after those changes are frozen, so a prompt improved by watching scores is never reported on the data it was fitted to.
_decoys: Plausible same-topic alternatives that did NOT come next. They join the candidate pool so discrimination tests specificity rather than topic recognition.

questions: what is Docker
how do Docker image layers work
how do I reduce the size of a Docker image
how do I stop secrets from ending up in an image layer
summaries: Docker packages an application with its dependencies into an image that runs identically wherever the runtime exists. Containers share the host kernel, making them much lighter than virtual machines.

An image is a stack of read-only layers, one per build instruction. Layers are cached and shared between images, so an unchanged instruction is not rebuilt. Changing an early layer invalidates everything after it.
Size comes down by using a smaller base image, combining RUN instructions so intermediate files do not persist, and using multi-stage builds so build tooling never reaches the final image.
decoys: how do I speed up Docker builds with better layer caching
should I use Alpine or Debian as a base image
how do I share a volume between two containers

questions: how does indexing work in Postgres
what is the difference between a B-tree and a GIN index
how do I tell whether Postgres is using my index
why does Postgres ignore my index on a small table
summaries: An index is a separate structure letting the planner find rows without scanning the table. Reads get faster, writes get slower, since every insert must maintain the index.

B-tree indexes suit ordered scalar comparisons and ranges. GIN indexes suit values containing many elements, such as arrays, JSONB documents, and full-text vectors, where a single row has many searchable keys.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the chosen plan and actual timings. An Index Scan or Bitmap Index Scan means the index is used; a Seq Scan means it was not.

questions: when should I use useState versus useReducer in React
why does my useEffect run twice
how do I stop a component re-rendering unnecessarily
how do I tell which prop is causing the re-render
summaries: useState suits independent values. useReducer suits several values that change together under named transitions, keeping update logic in one place instead of scattered setters.
React 18 Strict Mode mounts, unmounts, and remounts components in development to surface missing cleanup. The double invocation is intentional and does not happen in production builds.
Re-renders are reduced by memoizing components with React.memo, stabilizing callback and object identities, and lifting state no higher than it needs to live.

questions: what problem does Kubernetes solve
what is the difference between a pod and a deployment
how do liveness and readiness probes differ
why does my pod keep restarting after a failed probe
summaries: Kubernetes schedules containers across a cluster and keeps declared state true, restarting failures and rescheduling work when nodes die, rather than requiring manual placement.
A pod is one or more containers scheduled together as the smallest deployable unit. A deployment manages a replica set of identical pods and handles rolling updates and rollbacks.
A readiness probe controls whether a pod receives traffic. A liveness probe controls whether it is killed and restarted. Confusing them causes healthy-but-slow pods to be repeatedly killed.

questions: what is the difference between git merge and git rebase
how do I squash several commits into one
how do I recover a commit I deleted
how do I undo a rebase that went wrong
summaries: Merge preserves history and adds a merge commit. Rebase replays commits onto a new base, giving linear history but rewriting commit hashes, which is unsafe on shared branches.
Interactive rebase lets commits be marked squash or fixup so they collapse into one. The rewrite changes hashes, so the branch must be force-pushed afterwards.
The reflog records where HEAD has pointed, including commits no longer reachable from any branch, so a deleted commit can be found and restored for as long as it remains unpruned.
decoys: how do I rewrite an old commit message
when is force-pushing actually safe

questions: what makes a test suite reliable
what is the difference between a mock and a stub
why are my tests flaky
how do I find which test is polluting shared state
summaries: Reliability comes from tests that are deterministic, isolated from each other, and fast enough to run constantly. A slow or intermittent suite stops being trusted and then stops being run.
A stub returns canned values so code under test can proceed. A mock additionally asserts how it was called, which couples the test to implementation and breaks under refactoring.
Flakiness usually traces to shared mutable state between tests, real clocks and timers, unordered collections assumed ordered, or genuine concurrency races.
decoys: how much test coverage should I actually aim for
should I test private methods
how do I speed up a slow test suite

questions: what is the difference between authentication and authorization
how do JSON web tokens work
why should refresh tokens be rotated
where should I store a refresh token in a browser
summaries: Authentication establishes who a caller is. Authorization decides what that caller may do. Conflating them tends to produce systems where any logged-in user can reach anything.
A JWT carries signed claims, so a server validates it without a session lookup. That statelessness is also the drawback: a token stays valid until it expires unless a revocation list is maintained.
Rotation issues a new refresh token on each use and invalidates the old one, so a stolen token is detectable when both the attacker and the user present the same one.

what is the difference between OAuth and OpenID Connect

questions: what is a vector database
how does Chroma differ from Pinecone
how does HNSW indexing work
how do I choose a vector database for a small project
summaries: A vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings and indexes them so nearest-neighbour lookups stay fast as the collection grows. Queries are embedded too, and results ranked by distance rather than exact match.

Chroma is open-source and self-hosted, running in-process or as a small server, which suits local and small-scale work. Pinecone is a managed service that handles scaling and replication for you at the cost of hosting it yourself.

HNSW builds a layered navigable small-world graph, with sparse upper layers used for coarse routing and a dense base layer for refinement, giving approximate nearest-neighbour search in roughly logarithmic time.

questions: what is retrieval augmented generation
what chunking strategies work best for RAG
how do I evaluate a RAG pipeline
does adding a reranker improve RAG accuracy
summaries: RAG retrieves relevant documents and appends them to the prompt, so the model answers from supplied evidence rather than memorised weights. This grounds responses and allows citation without retraining.

Chunks must be small enough to retrieve precisely but large enough to stay coherent. Overlapping windows avoid cutting an idea in half, and splitting on document structure beats splitting on a fixed token count.

Retrieval and generation are measured separately, because a fluent answer can come from irrelevant context. Retrieval is scored with recall at k; generation is scored for faithfulness to the retrieved text.

questions: what is fine-tuning a language model
how does LoRA reduce fine-tuning cost
when should I fine-tune instead of using RAG
how much training data do I need to fine-tune effectively
summaries: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on a narrower dataset so it adapts to a domain, format, or style without learning language from scratch.

LoRA freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices injected into each layer. Only the adapters receive gradients, so optimiser state and memory drop sharply and adapters are a few megabytes.
Fine-tuning teaches form: tone, structure, and consistent output shape. RAG supplies facts. Knowledge that changes should live in retrieval, since retraining on every update is impractical.

questions: what is the difference between Playwright and Selenium
how do I reuse a logged-in browser session in Playwright
how do websites detect automated browsers
how do I keep a scraper working when a site changes its HTML
summaries: Playwright bundles its own browser builds and waits automatically for elements to become actionable. Selenium is older, drives browsers through separate WebDriver binaries, and leaves waiting to the caller.
A persistent context stores cookies and local storage on disk, so a session survives between runs. Saving and reloading a storage state file avoids logging in on every execution.
Detection uses navigator.webdriver, headless-specific rendering differences, timing that is too regular to be human, and TLS or HTTP fingerprints that differ from a real browser.

questions: how does the attention mechanism work in transformers
why do transformers need positional encoding
what does multi-head attention add over single-head
how does a KV cache speed up inference
summaries: Attention scores each token against every other using query and key projections, then takes a softmax-weighted sum of value vectors, letting any token draw information from anywhere in the sequence in one step.
Attention is permutation-invariant, so without positional information a shuffled sentence looks identical. Positional encodings inject order into the token representations before attention sees them.
Multiple heads attend in parallel subspaces, so one head can track syntax while another tracks coreference. Concatenating them gives richer representations than a single averaged attention pattern.

questions: what is tool calling in a language model
what is the ReAct pattern for agents
when is a multi-agent system better than a single agent
how do I benchmark an agent's task completion rate
summaries: Tool calling lets a model emit a structured function call instead of prose. The host executes it and returns the result as an observation, which the model continues from. This is the mechanism under most agent loops.
ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting: the model states a thought, takes an action, observes the result, and repeats. Making reasoning explicit between steps improves recovery from bad actions.
Multiple agents help when subtasks need genuinely different tools, context, or system prompts. When they share context, splitting mostly adds coordination overhead and duplicated understanding.

how should an agent recover from a failed tool call

questions: what is prompt caching
how does an LRU cache decide what to evict
what is cache invalidation and why is it hard
how do I stop a cache stampede when a hot key expires
summaries: Prompt caching stores the processed prefix of a prompt so repeated requests sharing that prefix skip recomputation, cutting latency and cost when a long system prompt is reused.
An LRU cache evicts the entry unused for longest, approximating the assumption that recently used items are likely to be used again. It is usually implemented with a hash map over a linked list.
Invalidation is hard because the cache must learn that source data changed, and the signal often arrives late, partially, or not at all, leaving stale reads that are difficult to detect.
